title: Round 16 - the cash constraint was worth nothing, and found a defect anyway
focus: Round 15 shipped every savings and Roth figure stamped cash_constraint_modelled: false, arguing they were systematically optimistic because the contribution harness always affords a rebalance a real account sometimes cannot - the real engine logged 58 insufficient_cash rejections over the same card and window. Round 16 built the constraint and measured the bias across all 31 contribution cells, paired, one variable.
headline: The bias is zero, not small: the cash constraint never binds once in 31 cells, so round 15's stated cause for the 0.66% divergence between its two paths was wrong.
outcome:
Zero underfunded buys across 31 cells, mean drag +0.000pp, and all 31 unconstrained cells reproduce round 15 exactly. The constraint is inert on this field of cards.

The reason, measured rather than assumed: two mechanisms already made the harness cash-safe. The contribution pre-buy step spends only min(cash, need) and could never overdraw. And the band-breach rebalance nets to zero across the book by construction - targets sum to at most 1 of equity - so with sells executing before buys, the proceeds are always there before the buys need them. The unconstrained path could overdraw only transiently, mid-loop, because it walked symbols in dict order and could buy before selling; netted across the session it always balanced. Ordering sells first removes the transient and changes no outcome, because the transient never had one.

So the 58 rejections are real and the inference drawn from them was not. Aggregate cash was never the binding constraint, and r15_control.py still reports 0.6567% unchanged. Whatever separates the two paths is something else - whole-share fills (the broker transacts shares, the harness transacts dollars), settlement lag (deliberately excluded from this round to keep one variable), or the decide-at-close fill-at-open lag. That the rejections coexist with zero aggregate shortfall is itself the clue: a broker rejecting a buy it cannot fund in whole shares at the open is not the same as a book that cannot fund it in dollars at the close.

Three of four pre-registered predictions were falsified outright and the fourth was half right. Prediction 4 had named its own consequence in advance - if the divergence stayed above 0.50%, settlement rather than the cash cap is the dominant term - so the round ends with a better hypothesis than it started with, which is the whole point of writing them down first.

The round also found a defect it was not looking for. Round 15's runner created one card_weight_fn per card and reused it across all five windows. An AllocationCard's closure is stateless, so all 26 allocation cells reproduced to the last digit. A LadderCard's closure is a state machine carrying armed rung depth and the cycle-starting high, so each window inherited the previous one's state. Isolated directly: a shared closure gives 11.63% then 26.52% on the same window; two fresh closures give 11.63% twice. Corrected, ladder-sso-vig-bnd's CAGR falls by up to 16 points, and h10y-1 is unchanged because it ran first with a fresh closure - the signature that confirms the cause rather than merely fitting it.

That falsifies round 15's claim that the card beat QQQ on return in two windows. Corrected, it never beat QQQ on either return or drawdown in any window - which strengthens round 15's P4 verdict while destroying its supporting discussion. Round 15's record carries a dated correction rather than a rewrite, and its original figures are kept at contributions/roth-CONTAMINATED-INVALID/, the convention round 11 used for the instrument D5 retired.
carries_forward: The 0.66% divergence is SETTLEMENT, confirmed same-day -- see this round's SELECTION.md follow-up. PaperBroker holds sale proceeds unspendable for settlement_days (paperbroker.py:260/412/439) and rejected 59 buys on insufficient_cash with fractional shares on and frictions zeroed, while round 16's own cash cap bound zero times across 31 cells. A cash cap without settlement is not the constraint a real account has. Suspect 1 (whole-share fills) was wrong when written -- r15_control.py already sets allow_fractional_shares=True; suspect 3 (fill lag) was tested and made the gap 1.9% worse. Next: give simulate a settlement lag and re-run, predicting the gap closes materially.

A LadderCard's card_weight_fn closure is a state machine; an AllocationCard's is stateless. Build a fresh closure per cell, never one reused across windows. The first window is always correct, which is exactly what makes this defect hard to see - and why the h10y-1 cell being unchanged was the evidence rather than an anomaly.

cash_constrained=True stays in the harness despite changing nothing. It costs one branch, it is proven inert on this field, and a card with a larger rebalance relative to its book may bind where these did not. An invariant that never fires today is cheap insurance; one nobody wrote is not.

A mechanism being real does not make it the cause. 58 insufficient_cash rejections genuinely happened, and the bias inferred from them was zero. Prefer measuring a suspected term over reasoning from the existence of its mechanism.
Nothing is promoted. Round 16 re-uses round 15's windows by design, so a paired comparison is explicitly not the second independent measurement PROTOCOL.md section 6(b) requires.
